errors.claim: The Sui dynasty's Grand Canal joined the Yellow and Yangtze basins, and 'After the Tang fell in 907, a Kaifeng and Hangzhou linked by that canal could be one economy' with the framing that China fractured in 316 and reunified 'each time'
errors.fix: The frame is loose: 1127 (Jin-Song split) was never reunified by the Song; the north-south division ended only with the Mongol conquest in 1279, so the count of 'reunified each time' is a simplification, not a serious error.

errors.claim: The Mongol rulers brought back state examinations in 1315, so even foreign rulers adopted the same reading list.
errors.fix: Correct date of revival, but the Yuan examinations were small and the Mongols had suspended them for decades; presenting this as evidence the Yuan fully adopted the canon overstates it.

errors.claim: Cao Cao's defeat at Red Cliffs 'stopped the north from reuniting China'; Western Jin 'briefly rejoined the pieces' in 265 when it absorbed Cao Wei's land.
errors.fix: Western Jin replaced Cao Wei in 265 and conquered Wu in 280; reunification occurred in 280, not 265.

grade.best: It combines geography (the open plain and canal), the Qin template, exams and the Mandate into a layered mechanism, and explicitly tests it against the long divisions with Red Cliffs, Fei River and Xiangyang.
grade.worst: It never cleanly states Ko, Koyama and Sng's argument that a single steppe threat favoured large centralised states, and it blurs the dates of reunification (265 versus 280) and the 1127 case.

errors.claim: Maurya lasted about 140 years while also 'barely 137 years (318 to 171 BCE by the Cliopatria record...)' and 'The Maurya hold at around 320-185 BCE is the first time one center reached both cores'
errors.fix: Minor internal inconsistency in dates (318 to 171 BCE is 147 years, not 137); Maurya conventionally c.322-185 BCE.

errors.claim: Mughals 'held both passes by 1707' and Gommans cited as 'Military labour market' view with 'The Indian Frontier (2002)' as a separate title
errors.fix: Gommans' works are Mughal Warfare (2002) and The Rise of the Indo-Afghan Empire (1995); 'The Indian Frontier (2002)' appears to be a garbled title. Also the 'military labour market' thesis is Kolff's, not Gommans'.

errors.claim: Tughlaq 1333 peak 'the closest India came to unity before the Mughals' while the answer elsewhere names Maurya as bigger
errors.fix: Acceptable simplification; no real error.

grade.best: A well-developed mechanism chain linking separate self-financing granary cores, the cost of carrying revenue and armies across the Deccan, and an overlordship political culture, with explicit links and honest hedging.
grade.worst: It omits the armed peasantry and open military labour market (Kolff) as a driver of cheap rebellion and new states, and misattributes the labour-market idea to Gommans, while the premise check is only implicit rather than stating clearly that India was repeatedly largely unified.

points.note: Industry made gap huge after 1800 but did not start it; sustained growth discussed, though it argues the lead began earlier, partly contrasting with rubric framing
Low Countries then England pulling ahead of Italy/south, with Pamuk cited
Black Death raised wages, north-west high-wage economy
Pomeranz vs Allen/Broadberry dating of the gap named and weighed
Atlantic trade, institutions (North-Weingast; Acemoglu not named), coal/steam mentioned via Pomeranz view

errors.claim: Real wages roughly rose by half or more in a few decades
errors.fix: English real wages rose substantially after 1348 but the size varies by series; 'half or more' is at the high end

errors.claim: Milan 2.5 million and Prague 910,000 in 1800 (flagged as suspect by the answer)
errors.fix: Milan was about 100-130k; the answer flags this itself but still presents index values like Antwerp 591,000 in 1800 and Amsterdam 220,000 as the north-west's rise, when Antwerp was about 50-60k

errors.claim: Black Death in Messina October 1347, Marseille November, Florence March 1348, Melcombe June
errors.fix: Dates are broadly right; no error

errors.claim: The medieval boom of 1000-1300 was mostly more people, not richer ones, and income first pulled ahead 1350-1500
errors.fix: Broadberry's accounts show some per-head growth in the high Middle Ages; stated too firmly, though defensible

grade.best: It links the Black Death wage shock to persistent income gains using Maddison series and then separates the medieval headcount boom from per-head growth, with competing views weighed.
grade.worst: It uses clearly unreliable city-size index values (Antwerp 591,000, Milan 2.5 million in 1800) as evidence and slightly overstates the case for a 1350-1500 start, underplaying the post-1800 sustained-growth point.

errors.claim: Mycenaean Greece by 1101 BCE (ends in 1101 BCE) as the collapse date
errors.fix: The Mycenaean palaces were destroyed or abandoned around 1200-1180 BCE (Pylos about 1180); 1101 is just an Atlas end date for the polity, which misleads about the timing of the collapse.

errors.claim: Nur Sherif and Amiet-style storm-of-quakes ideas
errors.fix: The earthquake storm hypothesis is by Nur and Cline (2000); 'Nur Sherif and Amiet' is garbled attribution.

errors.claim: Ugarit's last king sent a letter that his ships were away in Hatti while enemy ships had burned his cities (also placing the Ammurapi letter as a fleet-readiness failure at 1177)
errors.fix: Ammurapi's letters say his troops and ships were in Hatti and Lycia, a fair reading, but they are dated before Ugarit's destruction and not tied to the 1177 battle; the answer links them loosely.

grade.best: It frames the collapse as a cascading systems failure, linking drought, tin trade, palace centralisation and Egypt's Nile buffer, and weighs Cline, Kaniewski, Nur and Drews fairly.
grade.worst: It never clearly says the collapse was spread over decades rather than the single year 1177, and the Mycenaean date of 1101 BCE misplaces the palace destruction by about a century.

errors.claim: Constantine introduced the gold solidus around 309 ... for roughly 700 years it kept its weight
errors.fix: The solidus was introduced c. 309/310 at 72 to the pound, but the Byzantine coin was debased from the 11th century, so it held full weight for about 700 years (to c. 1030s) rather than staying stable throughout; this is roughly right, and the 'stable gold coin' framing in the short answer overstates it for the later empire.

errors.claim: Walls fell only to treachery of a different kind: in 1204 the Fourth Crusade and Venice ... sacked the city
errors.fix: The 1204 capture was a naval and land assault by the Crusaders and Venetians, not treachery; the walls were breached by assault from the sea side (Golden Horn).

errors.claim: Rome itself was sacked in 410 by Visigoths 'the first fall of the city in 800 years'; and in Step 7 the Dardanelles/Bosporus 'forced the Goths to roam the Balkans rather than cross into rich Anatolia'
errors.fix: The 410 sack date and 800-year gap are fine, but the straits claim is an inference; Goths were not mainly stopped by the straits. Treated as inference by the answer itself, so minor.

grade.best: It links geography, fiscal base, Africa's loss and court politics into a causal chain (e.g. the West's shrinking revenue leading to land-paid generals who controlled emperors) while naming Heather, Ward-Perkins and Luttwak views with honest unknowns.
grade.worst: It never challenges the premise that 476 was the 'fall' (a convention, with the West dissolving into successor kingdoms over decades) and the Black Death steps drift off the question into 1348 rather than answering why Rome fell.

errors.claim: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus ended in 401 CE by Christian-era dismantling rather than a quake; Goths wrecked it in 262 (the 268 date is the usual one)
errors.fix: Herostratus burned it in 356 BCE, it was rebuilt, and the Goths sacked it in 268 CE. The answer never mentions Herostratus or the rebuild, and its Goth date of 262 is off.

errors.claim: In 1406 the Knights of St John began building Bodrum Castle, and elsewhere 'from 1402'; the Mausoleum was quarried in 1522
errors.fix: Construction of Bodrum Castle began in 1402. The answer gives conflicting dates (1402, 1406, 1522), and 1522 is the date of the Knights' loss of Rhodes, not of quarrying the Mausoleum.

errors.claim: The Mausoleum's slabs reached the British Museum in 1846 and the Knights' 'final surrender at Rhodes' in 1522 ended their hold, so the site was left to be taken apart
errors.fix: The Knights held Bodrum until 1522 and the quarrying was largely in the 1400s-1500s. The timeline is muddled.

errors.claim: Qaitbay's fort rebuilt in 1477 and Ibn Battuta saw the ruin 'around 1326 and again in 1349'
errors.fix: Ibn Battuta visited in 1326 and 1349. This is roughly right, but the Lighthouse quake dates are stated with more certainty than the sources allow.

errors.claim: The Library of Alexandria's decline is attributed to Caesar's fire and ending of patronage, and described as a 'pagan site closing' in the wonders story
errors.fix: The Library was not one of the Seven Wonders. It is a tangent that muddies the answer.

errors.claim: Giza survived with 'its outer limestone casing stripped', yet the opening says all six were 'destroyed ... between 226 BCE and 1500s CE'
errors.fix: The dates are fine, but Ephesus and Olympia are said to be 'destroyed' by law when physical causes (Goths, floods, earthquakes) mattered more. This is a defensible simplification.

grade.best: It explains survival and loss through mechanisms (seismic ground, funding and upkeep, law and belief, reuse of stone), and it flags the Hanging Gardens as possibly never at Babylon, citing Dalley.
grade.worst: The Ephesus account omits Herostratus's arson in 356 BCE and the rebuild, and several dates are muddled (Goths 262, Bodrum 1402/1406/1522), with a tangent on the Library of Alexandria.

errors.claim: Ur's final abandonment around 450 BCE came as the river moved and the head of the Persian Gulf coast changed; Ur is described as a river city that vanished and Uruk 'ends 640 CE'
errors.fix: Ur's decline from drought and the Euphrates shifting is plausible, but the claim that the Gulf coastline changed is a contested older theory; coastline progradation is much smaller than once claimed.

errors.claim: Babylon, 100 km north on the Euphrates at the point where it comes closest to the Tigris
errors.fix: Babylon is about 85-100 km south of Baghdad; it is not 100 km north of Ur (it is roughly 300 km north-northwest). The 'closest to the Tigris' point is loosely stated.

errors.claim: Petra's toll dried up when 'Rome took over the Red Sea sea-lanes'; Petra 'gone as a city' by 700
errors.fix: Petra was annexed by Rome in 106 CE and thrived for centuries; its decline came from sea routes, Palmyra's rise and the 363 earthquake, not a sudden Roman takeover.

errors.claim: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa sit on 'monsoon-fed rivers' and the Ghaggar-Hakra shifted
errors.fix: Largely defensible but contested; presented as pattern though flagged as argued. Minor.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal framework (single-channel or single-commodity dependence versus a fallback site, plus sacred obligation) and supports it with climate, silt, trade and disease evidence while flagging inferences.
grade.worst: It should more squarely name the rubric's clearest vanished cases (Cahokia, Ctesiphon) and long-lived ones (Rome, Xi'an/Luoyang), and tighten loose claims about Petra and Babylon's geography.

errors.claim: Florence lost roughly half to three-fifths in 1348, yet the 1353 figure of 46,000 (down from 54,000) is 'plausible'; also the step 8 title 'Florence loses a third, Cologne gains a sixth'
errors.fix: The title contradicts the body text, which says Florence lost half to three-fifths; a drop from 54,000 to 46,000 is about 15% and is not plausible as the plague toll.

errors.claim: Cairo is listed at 443,000 in 1330 and 437,000 in 1353 ... 'the biggest city on the map was probably the biggest single loss'; Alexandria and Constantinople reached in 1347 with Messina and Alexandria both in October
errors.fix: Minor: Constantinople was hit in spring/summer 1347 and Messina in October 1347; the answer's chronology is broadly sound, but the claim of the largest single loss is speculative.

grade.best: It traces the route from the Chu valley through Caffa and the Mediterranean to the Baltic with careful hedging about the Caffa catapult story, the Chu link and transmission, and it ties scarcity to wages and the Statute of Labourers.
grade.worst: It omits the massacres of Jews blamed for the plague (Strasbourg 1349) and only vaguely sketches serfdom weakening in the west versus a second serfdom in the east, with no explicit mention of Genoese galleys reaching Messina as the entry point beyond a brief note.

errors.claim: Africa's population stagnated at around 100 million across the 1700s while the rest of the world grew
errors.fix: Africa's population is commonly estimated at roughly 100 million in 1700 and 100 million or somewhat more in 1800, but the figures are very uncertain; stating it as a settled stagnation overstates what is known.

grade.best: It links disease, succession crises, labor shortage, slavery, silver and crops into a causal chain, and it names the population uncertainty (8 to over 100 million) alongside rival scholars.
grade.worst: It barely covers the Old World animals and crops (horses, cattle, wheat) that transformed the Americas, such as the Plains horse cultures, and it gives the Great Dying as a precise 80 to 90 percent loss.

points.note: Network not one road, named Seidenstraße 1877 by Richthofen in the views

errors.claim: Tang-era shipwreck evidence, the Belitung wreck of about 830, shows Chinese ceramics going west by water
errors.fix: The Belitung wreck is dated to about 826-830 and is real; no error here, but it is Indonesian waters Arab dhow carrying Changsha ware, which supports the claim.

grade.best: It shows with causal links why geography (Taklamakan, steppe, monsoon) produced a braid of relayed routes and then ties trade, ideas and plague into one mechanism.
grade.worst: It spends over half its steps on the 1340s plague and gives little weight to the first-millennium Sogdian role and the Han-to-Tang period, and it gives Richthofen's 1877 naming only in the views section.

errors.claim: the Atlantic crossing was about a week, 'shorter than the flu's 2-day incubation plus 1 week of illness would need to outlast'; the ship could brew an outbreak at sea
errors.fix: Crossing took roughly 7-10 days, and the logic is garbled: a week-long crossing is comparable to or longer than incubation plus infectious period, which is why ships arrived with active outbreaks. The sentence's comparison is muddled, though the conclusion is plausible.

errors.claim: The virus came to Bombay with returning soldiers and sailors in late May and again in September 1918 (step 8), and 'arrived in Bombay by ship in June 1918' (step 3), with India's toll of 12-17 million vs 12-20 million elsewhere
errors.fix: Bombay arrival is usually dated to late May/June 1918 with the deadly wave arriving in September; the answer is internally inconsistent on dates and toll ranges, but is not clearly wrong.

errors.claim: Chandra, Kuljanin and Wray cited as 'Mortality from the influenza pandemic of 1918-19 in Indonesia', Population Studies, 2012 for India's death toll
errors.fix: That paper concerns Indonesia; the India paper is Chandra, Kuljanin and Wray's 'Reassessing the Indian 1918 Influenza Pandemic' (Demography, 2012). The answer cites both inconsistently.

errors.claim: Camp Devens near Boston saw roughly 14,000 cases within weeks; the AEF shipped about two million men to France
errors.fix: Broadly accurate; no correction needed.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal chain from wartime logistics, censorship and a short infectious period to rapid global spread, supported by the Samoa natural experiment, while keeping the origin explicitly unsettled.
grade.worst: It never states clearly the W-shaped mortality curve for young adults, treating the young-adult pattern only in passing, and it has a mismatched citation for the Indian estimates.

errors.claim: Srivijaya (674 to 1293 CE) ... The Chola raid of 1025 'broke' Srivijaya; Chola peak 1028; also the Delhi/Vijayanagara and Mamluk dates inconsistent (Mamluk Sultanate 1250-1517 in step 6, 1241 to 1518 in step 11)
errors.fix: The answer gives inconsistent Mamluk dates (1250-1517 vs 1241-1518); the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo is conventionally 1250-1517. Also the Chola raid weakened but did not end Srivijaya.

errors.claim: The Mozambique Channel offered no reliable return wind, which helps explain why Kilwa, not Great Zimbabwe's coast, became the gold exit
errors.fix: Great Zimbabwe is inland; gold left via Sofala, which the answer itself mentions in step 7. Kilwa's rise is better explained by control of the Sofala gold trade, and the Mozambique Channel claim is speculative.

errors.claim: Cargo arrived on the southwest monsoon at Aden, went up the Red Sea ... (and step 4: summer southwest monsoon carried ships east to India, northeast brought them home)
errors.fix: The direction is muddled: ships from the Arabian side typically sailed to India on the southwest monsoon and returned on the northeast, but step 1 says the northeast carries ships from Arabia and India toward Africa. The directions are consistent in themselves yet the Aden claim is loosely stated.

grade.best: It explains the mechanism clearly as a causal chain: reversing winds, one round trip a year, forced waiting, then ports, credit, diasporas and tolls, with Srivijaya and Mamluk Cairo as concrete cases.
grade.worst: It omits the ancient Greco-Roman Red Sea to Muziris trade (Periplus) and the 1498 arrival of da Gama at Calicut with a local pilot and the Portuguese attempt to seize control, and it spends heavy space on the Black Death, which the question did not ask about.

errors.claim: Musa's hajj ran roughly 6,000 km or more each way from the Niger bend to Cairo and on to Mecca
errors.fix: The route from the Niger bend to Cairo is roughly 4,000-5,000 km, and Mecca adds more; 6,000 km each way to Cairo is overstated (flagged as the answer's own estimate).

errors.claim: Musa's realm was 'bigger than anything in the Atlas's window except Mamluk Egypt and the Byzantines'
errors.fix: Mali was far larger than the Byzantine empire of 1324, which was a small rump state; the comparison is wrong.

grade.best: It separates what is well attested (al-'Umari's report of the dinar's fall in Cairo, the Catalan Atlas image) from second-hand figures, and explains Mali's wealth as rationing and taxing the gold-salt exchange rather than mining.
grade.worst: It treats Timbuktu and Djenne as centres of trade and learning only thinly, saying Timbuktu's fame came later and not clearly tying Djenne to Islamic scholarship, and it includes a questionable claim that Mali was larger than the Byzantines.

errors.claim: Congo-Angola coast alone supplied roughly 5.7 million of the embarked (step 1), alongside 'perhaps 45 percent' of captives from West Central Africa
errors.fix: West-Central Africa embarked about 5.7 million, roughly 45 percent of the 12.5 million; this is broadly consistent, so no real error.

errors.claim: Southeast Africa to Brazil by the Cape adds a voyage of 12,000 km-plus; Angola to Brazil is about 6,000 km versus 8,000+ to the Caribbean
errors.fix: Distances are rough; Angola to Brazil is shorter than to the Caribbean, but figures are approximate rather than clearly wrong.

grade.best: It gives the Voyages totals (12.5 million embarked, 10.7 million landed, one in seven dying) and correctly explains that Brazil and the Caribbean, not North America, received nearly all captives, with wind systems and sugar as causes.
grade.worst: It never clearly states that the trade peaked in the 18th century, so the timing point is only implied through sugar, and the error list should be tightened to avoid hedged claims.

errors.claim: Hartwell's 125,000 tonnes is 'of the same order as Europe's total output many centuries later' and the 'Gaoliang River 979 ... near today's Beijing' fine, but 'Jurchen Jin ... who had been Song allies against Liao' with 'two emperors captured' in 1126-27
errors.fix: The two-emperor capture is correct; however the claim that the 1005 Chanyuan treaty paid 100,000 taels silver and 200,000 bolts silk is correct only as 100,000 taels and 200,000 bolts, so no error there. The real issue is that the Mongols conquered Jin in 1234 and Kaifeng fell in 1233, while the answer says Caizhou 1233 ended Jin; Jin ended at Caizhou in 1234.

errors.claim: Examinations were suspended under the Yuan for decades, resuming in 1315
errors.fix: Correct in outline; but the claim the Yuan dynasty began '1294 onward' is wrong: Yuan was proclaimed in 1271 and Kublai's reign ran to 1294.

errors.claim: Jiaozi became a state issue 'around 1024' because iron coin was too heavy
errors.fix: Correct; but 'Quanzhou (1000-1400)' and 'Song paper money among the first' are fine. The statement that Champa rice or similar is missing is an omission, not an error.

grade.best: It weighs Elvin, Hartwell, Allen and Pomeranz against each other, ties the 1127 loss of the northern coal-iron belt to the state-as-customer argument, and states its uncertainty openly.
grade.worst: It never mentions fast-ripening Champa rice or the agricultural revolution behind the Song boom, and its few date slips (Yuan 'from 1294', Jin ending 1233 rather than 1234) need correcting.

errors.claim: Karakorum (founded 1220) / Atlas border layer shows Mongol Empire gains 4.5 million km² in 1220 and 5.5 million km² by 1227
errors.fix: Karakorum was founded as a camp c. 1220 but built up under Ögedei in the 1230s; the area figures are presented without hedging, though only a modest issue. Merv-type precise areas are model outputs.

errors.claim: The Hungarian Plain's pasture could support only some 30,000 horses (Peter Brecke / ecological-limit school)
errors.fix: The pasture-limit hypothesis is from Károly Állan/Zsolt Pinter-style modelling (Hungarian researchers, e.g. Sinor and Pow), not Peter Brecke; attribution is shaky.

grade.best: It links steppe grass, decimal army and keshig, siege specialists, the yam and terror-as-price-list into a coherent mechanism chain and openly hedges inflated numbers and the contested Hungary withdrawal.
grade.worst: It misses the climate factor (the wet, mild 1211-25 period behind horse fodder) and gives little on the empire splitting into four khanates and the Yuan conquest of Song China by 1279.

errors.claim: Thessaloniki ... was also lost to Ottoman rule in this period [by 1400], yet later 'a city, Thessaloniki and the Morea' still ruled by Byzantium at 1400
errors.fix: Thessaloniki was Ottoman from 1387, returned 1403, then sold to Venice in 1423 and taken by the Ottomans in 1430; the answer's account is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: the garrison of about 7,000 held 'some 20 km of walls' and elsewhere 'about 6.5 km' of land front
errors.fix: The total circuit is about 20 km including sea walls and the land wall about 6.5 km; the framing is confusing but not wrong in itself.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain (lost hinterland, thin garrison, fiscal capacity for Orban's guns, Lycus breach, ships overland) and explicitly weighs 1453 against Portuguese expansion as an accelerant, not the cause.
grade.worst: It never says that Greek scholars carried manuscripts to Italy or links 1453 to the Renaissance, and it gives Byzantium's population only indirectly rather than stating it was a tiny rump of a few tens of thousands.

errors.claim: Cusco, 'founded from 1100' / 'sat at the top' and Chan Chan's end in 1470 with Inca empire peak and the empire 'grew roughly 30-fold in about 60 years'
errors.fix: Cusco's founding date is traditional and uncertain; the 30-fold growth claim is a loose estimate. Minor, defensible simplification.

errors.claim: Relay runners 'waited at huts roughly every 2 to 2.5 km' and a message could cover 'on the order of 200 km a day'
errors.fix: Chasqui stations were typically about 2.5 km (1.5 miles) apart, and 240 km/day is the usual figure; stated roughly and hedged, so near correct.

grade.best: It ties khipu, mit'a labour, qollqa storehouses, roads and mitmaq into one coherent system and links its strengths to its fragility, with Murra, Urton and D'Altroy weighed fairly.
grade.worst: Pachacuti's rapid expansion from about 1438 is only implicit and the civil war and smallpox sequence is scattered across steps; a tighter, explicit timeline and a clearer statement that the 1532 conquest came after smallpox and civil war would help.

errors.claim: Cortés had left Tenochtitlan in the Noche Triste retreat of 30 June 1520, and the virus stayed behind (smallpox arrived with Narváez's men, who came before the Noche Triste, with the epidemic mainly erupting after the retreat)
errors.fix: The Noche Triste was a flight from Tenochtitlan; the smallpox epidemic broke out in the city mainly after the Spaniards' expulsion (autumn 1520). The framing is a little muddled, but not clearly wrong.

errors.claim: Cholula is described as a 'Tlaxcalan-adjacent holy city' that was massacred and showed the Spaniards could break an Aztec-linked center; the massacre is said to rest partly on Malinche's warning of an ambush
errors.fix: The Cholula massacre was carried out with Tlaxcalan allies; the ambush claim comes from Spanish sources and is contested as a justification. Presented with mild hedging, so minor.

errors.claim: Cuitlahuac 'ruled for about 80 days' after Moctezuma II's death and died in 'late 1520'
errors.fix: Cuitlahuac ruled about 80 days, but Moctezuma died in late June 1520 and Cuitlahuac died around December 1520 (some sources say roughly Nov-Dec); 80 days from late June would end in September, so the chronology is slightly inconsistent.

errors.claim: Step 3: 'Spaniards ... Tlaxcalans were presumably also struck' and 'the Spanish and their allies were largely not hit as hard', with 'some Spaniards had immunity from childhood exposure'
errors.fix: Smallpox did not exist in Spain as a universal childhood exposure issue in a way that is documented here; many Spaniards had prior exposure to smallpox in Europe, which is broadly accurate, so this is a defensible claim and not a clear error.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal chain linking tribute fragility, Tlaxcalan defection, Malinche's diplomacy, smallpox decapitation and the lake siege, while explicitly treating technology as the keystone rather than the arch.
grade.worst: Tighten the chronology around Cuitlahuac's reign and the smallpox timeline, and weigh Restall and Townsend more directly rather than leaving the Indigenous-agency argument mostly in one view.

errors.claim: Princip's driver took a wrong turn onto Franz Josef Street, stalled at Schiller's delicatessen, and Princip 'stood two meters away'; Berlin's 'Sazonov and Janushkevich' pressed Nicholas as 'his generals'
errors.fix: Sazonov was Russia's foreign minister, not a general; Janushkevich was chief of the General Staff. Calling Sazonov a general is wrong.

errors.claim: The Archduke's death 'Nicholas ordered general mobilization on 29 July, then cancelled it that night after Wilhelm's telegram'
errors.fix: Nicholas cancelled the general mobilization order after Wilhelm's telegram on 29 July, which is broadly right, but Wilhelm's telegram was not the only cause; minor nuance, not a serious error.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain from Balkan nationalism through the blank cheque, the Schlieffen clock and Russian mobilisation, and explicitly says mobilisation did not make war literally automatic while weighing Fischer, Clark and Taylor.
grade.worst: It never clearly explains how the two alliance blocs (Entente and Central Powers) widened a Balkan war into a continental one, and it gives no weight to Britain's entry beyond the Belgium geography.

errors.claim: Hideyoshi's army had to retreat from Korea in 1598, so Japan's coast felt safe; Korea Strait is about 190 km from Busan to Fukuoka with roughly 50 km of it dotted with Tsushima
errors.fix: Busan to Tsushima is about 50 km and Tsushima to Fukuoka about 130 km; the framing is muddled but roughly fine. Minor, not a real error.

errors.claim: roughly 18 to 20 million koku nationwide by the early 1600s, while step 5 says roughly 30 million koku with the shogunate holding about 4 million
errors.fix: Japan's total was about 18-20 million koku c. 1600 (about 30 million by the 1800s); the answer is internally inconsistent, and the shogunate's direct holdings were roughly 4 million koku.

grade.best: It builds a real causal chain in which Hideyoshi's disarmament, the daimyo sorting, sankin-kotai, the Edo and Osaka market and ideology reinforce one another, and it frames the settlement as a bargain that left the tozama armed.
grade.worst: Fix the inconsistent koku totals (18-20 million versus 30 million) and say more clearly that the end came with Perry's 1853 arrival, which is only briefly mentioned in the unknowns.

errors.claim: The Act's occupation rule applied only to coasts, which left the interior open to paper claims (and 'required a power taking a coast to notify')
errors.fix: This is accurate as to the Act's text; however, the claim that Italian Africa 'only appears from 1890 and peaks decades later in 1940' is fine. No error here.

errors.claim: Ethiopia's abolition of slavery listed as 1942 and Tunisia 1846 used to show Africans and Ottomans had 'their own paths' while Europeans justified conquest as ending slavery
errors.fix: Dates are plausible; not an error. Real issue is the rinderpest source line 'Charles H. Ford? no; John Ford' is a visible drafting slip, not a factual error.

errors.claim: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 and the 1885 border change moved 5.1 million km² from Egypt into British Africa
errors.fix: Egypt's Sudan holdings were lost after the Mahdist revolt; the transfer to British Africa was not a clean 1885 transfer of 5.1 Mkm² (Sudan was held by the Mahdist state until 1898).

grade.best: It explicitly corrects the Berlin myth (no map was drawn there, it wrote procedure) and builds a layered causal chain from quinine, steamers and the Maxim gun through cheap concession-company claims to bilateral treaties.
grade.worst: Liberia's survival is only briefly explained and the 'only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent by 1914' point is never stated outright, and a few shaky details (the 1885 border-change figure, a visible 'Charles H. Ford? no' citation slip) need cleaning up.

points.note: League's mandate and Jinnah's bargaining discussed (view, step 2) but the 1940 Lahore Resolution is never mentioned

errors.claim: The Punjab Boundary Force, created 1 August with roughly 23,000 men... had to cover 12 districts
errors.fix: The force was about 50,000 men (some accounts 55,000) covering 12 districts; 23,000 is too low, though the answer flags it as from memory

errors.claim: Radcliffe had about five weeks to draw 'two commissions' worth of borders'... 'Lahore went to Pakistan, and its Hindu and Sikh population fled in weeks'; the line fell 'between Lahore and Amritsar'
errors.fix: Broadly fine; no error. (Not counted.)

errors.claim: The Rule: Mountbatten announced on 3 June a handover for 15 August, 'about ten weeks away'
errors.fix: 3 June to 15 August is about ten and a half weeks; acceptable. The 3 June plan announced the partition scheme, and the 15 August date was named at the press conference on 4 June. Minor.

grade.best: It links the mechanism of the rushed handover (compressed timetable, late-published Radcliffe line, a divided army with no force able to protect people) to the violence, and weighs Jalal, Khan and Pandey fairly with honest unknowns.
grade.worst: It omits the 1940 Lahore Resolution and the sequence of Jinnah's Pakistan demand, so the political origin of the partition demand is thin, and it adds the Punjab Boundary Force strength wrong.

errors.claim: a newly unified Arabian coalition struck just after their 603-628 war (also 'peace in 603', 'war of 603-628', '26 years of war (602-628)')
errors.fix: The war began in 602 (Maurice's murder) and ended 628; the answer is inconsistent (602 vs 603), a minor dating slip.

errors.claim: Ctesiphon fell about 637, and the Sasanian court retreated... the Sasanian Empire disappears after 643 / 'Sasanian Empire (224–651)'
errors.fix: Ctesiphon fell in 637 correctly, but the answer's dates for the empire's end vary (643 vs 651); the dynasty ended with Yazdegerd III's death in 651.

errors.claim: Kairouan founded in 670 and Carthage fell in 698; Alexandria fell around 641-642
errors.fix: These are broadly correct; no error. (Not counted.)

grade.best: It cleanly separates fast conquest from slow conversion, linking exhausted empires, light surrender terms, and the fiscal brake on conversion (Bulliet, jizya) in a coherent causal chain.
grade.worst: It never states clearly the full list of key victories (Egypt 641, Nahavand 642 only in passing) or the 711 Indus reach alongside Iberia, and it has inconsistent dates for the war (602/603) and the end of the Sasanians.

errors.claim: Taiho Code (701) set up Nara (710) as a Tang-style capital... Tang Code (624)
errors.fix: Broadly fine; but 'Huichang suppression ... in the 840s destroyed monastic estates' is fine. The more doubtful claim is that Nalanda fell 'around 1197' and 'around 1200' inconsistently; the standard date is c.1193 (Khilji).

errors.claim: Faxian returned from Sri Lanka by sea about 412 CE to Guangzhou
errors.fix: Faxian's return voyage ended in Shandong (near Qingzhou/Laoshan), not Guangzhou.

grade.best: It builds a clear causal chain linking narrow patronage, the shift of trade hubs, Hindu absorption and a concentrated monastic base, and it weighs the gradual-decline thesis against the invasion thesis explicitly.
grade.worst: Ashoka's role in spreading Buddhism abroad is barely made (the Ashoka step focuses on governance and 'no state church'), and the Nalanda date is given inconsistently as c.1193/1197/1200 instead of anchoring on Bakhtiyar Khilji c.1193.

grade.best: It links the economic, military and political lenses into one causal chain, running from the silver drain through the court's divided response to steamers flanking forts and cutting the Grand Canal, and it shows the mechanism at each link.
grade.worst: The short answer's claim that Britain never fought the Qing army on land is overstated, since the war included land battles at Chinhai, Chapoo and Chinkiang. The answer is also very long and repeats the Nemesis and Zhenjiang points across several steps.

errors.claim: Beauvais, the tallest choir attempt at about 48 m, fell in 1284 and was never completed (framed in step 6 as a result of stalled growth/population after the Black Death)
errors.fix: Beauvais collapsed in 1284 because of structural overreach, decades before the 1348 plague; it was not caused by population stalling.

errors.claim: Noyon began within about 30 years of Notre-Dame and Sens in the same belt, with Sens 'begun c.1135-40'; also 'Chartres' main fabric rose in roughly 25 years' vs 'within about 30 years' (inconsistent)
errors.fix: Chartres was rebuilt mainly c.1194-1220s; the answer gives two differing durations. Minor inconsistency, not a major error.

errors.claim: Paris at 124,000 in 1220 (used as evidence of a crowded city)
errors.fix: Realistic estimates for Paris c.1200 are around 25,000-50,000 (up to ~80,000 by 1300); the answer flags the figure as uncertain, but it is much too high.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain that links surplus, political need, and Suger's theology of light, and weighs von Simson, Panofsky, Duby and the political school fairly, including what each cannot explain.
grade.worst: Treat Beauvais as a structural limit of the style rather than a casualty of population stagnation, and drop or heavily caveat the implausible 124,000 figure for Paris.

errors.claim: Paper had reached Baghdad by 794 and Xàtiva by 1056, so Europe was 1,100 years behind China (Luoyang 105)
errors.fix: Paper reached Spain (Xàtiva) around the 11th-12th century, but Europe was not 1,100 years behind in adopting it; Fabriano papermaking dates to 1276, about 1,170 years after 105 only if counting from China's invention, which is a muddled framing.

errors.claim: Venice had printed some 150 presses' worth of titles by 1500, including bankruptcies of Fust's rivals as Gutenberg's own financier
errors.fix: Garbled: Fust was Gutenberg's financier who foreclosed on him; he was not a victim of Venetian overproduction and Venetian bankruptcies were unrelated.

errors.claim: By 1500 an estimated 20 million books had been printed in Europe in about 1,000 presses' output
errors.fix: Febvre and Martin's estimate of roughly 20 million copies by 1500 is cited, but the 'about 1,000 presses' phrasing is vague; presses operated in about 250 towns.

errors.claim: Hangul (1443) / (1446) and Jikji printed in 1377 with 'Jikji ... Joseon' bureau Jujaso founded 1403 with state ministry control
errors.fix: Dates are defensible, but the Jikji was produced in Goryeo, not Joseon, and the answer slips between Hangul 1443 and 1446 inconsistently.

errors.claim: Economist step uses the map year 1348 and the Black Death as a driver of Gutenberg's press a century later
errors.fix: The labour-shortage causation is a contested hypothesis stated with more confidence than evidence supports.

grade.best: It explains the speed difference through linked mechanisms (alphabet and fixed-cost type, cheap paper, political fragmentation, state-held type in Korea and a single empire in China) and makes the cross-step links explicit.
grade.worst: It never names the Eisenstein versus Adrian Johns debate on how revolutionary print really was, and omits the Ottoman Muteferrika 1727 contrast, so the weighing of the 'print revolution' claim itself is thin.

errors.claim: Paper reached Samarkand in 751, Baghdad in 794, Cairo c.900, Xàtiva 1056, Fabriano 1276 alongside 'Bi Sheng-era Kaifeng had movable type by 1040'
errors.fix: Broadly accepted dates; however Fabriano's mill claim is fine. No clear error here.

errors.claim: Copernicus (1543) and Vesalius (1543) published in Nuremberg and Basel, outside any single censor's reach
errors.fix: Copernicus's De revolutionibus was printed in Nuremberg and Vesalius's Fabrica in Basel, so this is correct; but the implication that this was a free-from-censor choice is simplified.

errors.claim: The Dutch printed Galileo's Discorsi in 1638 at Leiden
errors.fix: Correct (Elzevir, Leiden). Not an error.

errors.claim: Magna Carta (1215) and the Golden Bull of 1222 are visible law tokens of corporations with legal personality
errors.fix: Magna Carta bound the king to barons and the Church; it did not establish corporate personality for towns or universities. The Golden Bull of 1222 is Hungarian, not tied to the Holy Roman Empire. Linking these to university autonomy is a loose argument.

grade.best: It names an institutional mechanism (chartered corporations plus fragmented jurisdictions that made exit cheap) with concrete cases such as Galileo, Paris 1277 and Taqi al-Din, and hedges the causal weights honestly.
grade.worst: It engages the Needham framing only through a view card and never directly says the question itself is contested, and it gives little detail on Copernicus, Galileo and Newton's Principia as the actual outcomes, or on the Tusi couple's role in Copernicus beyond a passing hint.

errors.claim: The Code of 529 was swiftly replaced by a revised one in 534, and the Institutes appeared in 533 as a student textbook; Digest 'boiled down' to about 50 books while Tribonian was 'dismissed after the Nika riot of 532 for corruption'
errors.fix: Tribonian was dismissed in 532 after the Nika riot and reinstated about 535; this is broadly right, but 'ten years of law in three' and the claim that 3 million lines were cut to 150,000 are traditional figures from the Digest preface, not firm counts

grade.best: It explicitly corrects the 'first code' assumption by naming Ur-Namma and Lipit-Ishtar, and ties each shift in authorship to a cause (royal legitimacy, debt crises, imperial restoration).
grade.worst: It never states that Hammurabi's penalties varied by social class (free man, commoner, slave), and it gives the Bologna rediscovery only as a passing aside rather than explaining how the Corpus shaped European civil law.

errors.claim: Domestication on the Pontic-Caspian steppe (Botai herding c. 3500 BCE, the modern lineage c. 2200 BCE) fed the spoked-wheel chariot
errors.fix: Botai is in Kazakhstan, not the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and Botai horses were not ancestors of the modern domestic lineage, so they did not feed the chariot's development; the answer elsewhere acknowledges this but the short answer blurs it.

errors.claim: Alexander's Companions rode without stirrups and fought with the sarissa-style xyston, with Darius's scythed chariots at Gaugamela failing against Alexander's infantry and Companion cavalry
errors.fix: The xyston was the Companions' lance; the sarissa was the infantry pike. Calling the xyston 'sarissa-style' is loose but defensible.

errors.claim: The tech layer shows iron smelting at Kaman-Kalehöyük around 2000 BCE
errors.fix: Kaman-Kalehöyük's iron dates to about 1800-1700 BCE at earliest for worked iron; 2000 BCE is early. Systematic iron smelting came about 1200-1000 BCE.

errors.claim: The Hittites at Hattusa were fielding chariots by the 1600s BCE and Egypt's Avaris/Hattusa chariots by 1650 BCE
errors.fix: Chariots reached Egypt with the Hyksos about 1600-1550 BCE; 1650 BCE for Avaris is slightly early but defensible.

grade.best: It links the chariot to its economic and political cost, showing the chariot-lord states as a brittle capital-intensive system that cheap iron and cavalry then displaced, and it is candid about which claims are inference or debated.
grade.worst: It never connects steppe horse-and-chariot migration (Yamnaya, c. 3000 BCE) to the spread of Indo-European languages, and its treatment of steppe cavalry peoples such as the Scythians is thin.

errors.claim: Hedeby sits where Jutland is narrowest, about 15 km of land between the Schlei and rivers flowing west; a shallow-draft longship could reach Paris 200 km from the sea
errors.fix: Paris is roughly 200 km upriver by the Seine, which is fine, but the Paris 'index: 250 BCE onward' aside is harmless; no clear error here, so this is not counted.

grade.best: It explains causes through linked mechanisms (political push, silver demand, geography, population limits) and ties the eastern dirham flow to the western raids.
grade.worst: The 1021 dated wood evidence at L'Anse aux Meadows is missing (it gives only 'c.1000'), and Iceland's 874 date is given only as an index value, so the settlement chronology is slightly imprecise.

errors.claim: Tikal fell to Calakmul's allies in 562, then in 695 Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil beat Calakmul
errors.fix: Broadly correct, but 'Tikal's last dated monument is about 869' and 'Tikal alive from -400 to 900' are fine; the one real slip is that the 800s-900s records are said to show earlier dry spells at 530-600, which is the Hiatus drought evidence, not the Cariaco 800-900s record, a minor conflation.

grade.best: It builds a layered causal chain in which drought struck a dense, rain-fed population and war-weakened divine kingship, while explaining the north's survival through cenotes and different rule, and it names Haug, Demarest and Diamond as competing views with fair weighting.
grade.worst: The errors list is thin; the answer could be tightened by clarifying the 530-600 drought claim and by stating more directly that the Maya people persist today, rather than only implying it through emigration and northern continuity.

errors.claim: Lapita 'covered about 4,000 km to Tonga and Samoa' and the first leap 'from the Bismarcks over some 3,000 km of island chain' (also 'roughly 4,500 km' in step 10)
errors.fix: The distances are inconsistent across steps; the Bismarcks to Samoa is roughly 4,000 km, and the 'first leap' was a series of short hops, not one 3,000 km leap.

errors.claim: Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa are 'the three points 7,000-8,000 km apart' and Rapa Nui settled c. 1200 as part of a single burst with Tonga-Samoa 'paused 1,500-2,000 years'
errors.fix: The triangle's corners are roughly 7,000-8,000 km apart, which is fine, but the pause is about 1,500-2,000 years only by older chronologies, and it is not the exact length of the gap between 800 BCE and 1000-1200 CE (about 1,800-2,000 years).

errors.claim: The Societies were reached 'at about 1025-1120 CE' and Rapa Nui's founding group is 'low dozens'
errors.fix: The Wilmshurst dates for the Societies are roughly 1025-1120 CE, which is acceptable. The 'low dozens' founding estimate for Rapa Nui is uncertain, and some studies suggest a larger group.

errors.claim: Ioannidis 2020 shows a contact dated 'about 1200 CE' with Zenú of Colombia, and the answer treats the direction as unknown
errors.fix: This is broadly correct. However, step 6 says that Black Death did not reach the Pacific and 'European contact in the 1600s-1700s' is accurate for Guam and Tahiti, so there is no error here.

grade.best: It explains the pause and burst through wind geometry, return-capable navigation and climate windows, weighs competing views and flags what is unproven.
grade.worst: Navigation is only treated in passing (single-hulled versus double-hulled voyaging canoes are never described), and the answer has several inconsistent distance figures and a garbled Lipson citation.

errors.claim: The Semmering line (1854) ... 14 tunnels and 16 viaducts
errors.fix: The Semmering railway has about 14 tunnels and 16 viaducts (plus many smaller bridges); the figure is roughly right, but it climbs about 460 m over 41 km, so this is acceptable. No clear error.

errors.claim: Paris to Constantinople on the Orient Express in about three days, ~2,900 km, or roughly 900 km a day
errors.fix: The journey took about 3 days (67 hours in 1889), but 2,900 km over 3 days is about 970 km/day, and the average includes stops and overnight running. Fair rounding, but the 'average per day' claim is loose.

errors.claim: Liverpool-Manchester railway ran at about 30 mph and the Atlas dates railways to Stockton-on-Tees in 1825 and Manchester in 1830, framing the L&M as a template without stating it was the first intercity line run entirely by steam
errors.fix: The L&M (1830) was the first intercity railway with steam locomotives only and a timetable; the answer omits this distinction.

grade.best: It quantifies the jump from tens of kilometres to several hundred a day and ties it to freight cost collapse, armies, and commuting, while noting the army still marched 30 km/day beyond the railhead.
grade.worst: It never mentions transcontinental lines (US 1869, Trans-Siberian) or railway time and time zones, and does not clearly state the Liverpool and Manchester line was the first all-steam intercity railway.

errors.claim: Lidar is not cited; Evans et al. 2007/2013 are credited with finding breached and blocked channels around the Angkor water network, and the view cites a 2007 PNAS paper with the 2013 title
errors.fix: The 'comprehensive archaeological map' paper is Evans et al. PNAS 2013 (lidar-based); the 2007 paper was a different one (radar mapping)

errors.claim: Quanzhou and Guangzhou 'under the Yuan and early Ming' fed trade, and Malacca became a hub from 1400 as the new gateway
errors.fix: Malacca was founded c. 1400 and only rose to a major entrepôt in the 15th century, so it was not yet a gateway when Angkor declined; minor chronology overstatement

grade.best: It treats the 'abandonment' as a slow relocation, weighs climate, Ayutthaya, trade and politics against each other, and notes that Angkor Wat stayed a living monastery.
grade.worst: It never cites the lidar finding of roughly 1,000 km² explicitly or uses it, and the Phnom Penh trade-pull argument leans on inference without data, so quantify scale and tighten the dating of the court's move.

errors.claim: Gerald Caton-Thompson / Africanist consensus (view attributed as 'Gerald Caton-Thompson')
errors.fix: The archaeologist is Gertrude Caton-Thompson, who in 1929 concluded the site was African-built.

grade.best: It gives a well-evidenced causal chain linking thin granite soils, cattle and fuelwood strain, and northward-shifting gold routes to a gradual abandonment, while openly flagging what is inferred and unsettled.
grade.worst: It barely addresses the colonial denial of African authorship and Rhodesian suppression of archaeologists, mentioning only that Phoenician/Arab myths persist in popular culture, and it misnames Gertrude Caton-Thompson.

errors.claim: Between roughly 2600 and 1700 BCE the Indus cities shrank and urban life dissolved (frame); also Harappa 'founded about 2600 BCE' and 'Mohenjo-daro's last phases show crowding and neglect'
errors.fix: 2600 BCE is the start of the Mature phase, and decline began after about 1900 BCE; the frame conflates the whole urban span with decline. Minor, though, and the short answer gives the correct 1900-1700 window.

errors.claim: Madhav Possehl and Cameron Petrie both read this as ruralization
errors.fix: The scholar is Gregory L. Possehl; 'Madhav Possehl' is a garbled name.

errors.claim: tuberculosis, found at Indus sites like Lothal-era sites
errors.fix: Evidence of tuberculosis (and leprosy) is reported at Harappan sites such as Lothal and Harappa; the phrasing is muddled but the claim is not clearly wrong.

grade.best: It separates what is supported (gradual ruralization, monsoon weakening, no invasion or massacre) from what is unsettled, flags 100-200 year dating errors, and shows how river-shift and climate explanations may be one mechanism.
grade.worst: It never states clearly in the short answer that the Indus script is undeciphered, so we have no written account, which is the central reason the cause remains uncertain.

errors.claim: Ptolemy's small Earth and shrunken degree: 'he shrank the degree to about 500 stadia' and Columbus used Ptolemy's small Earth, with Alfraganus's degree in Italian miles
errors.fix: Ptolemy used Posidonius's smaller circumference (180,000 stadia, ~500 stadia per degree), which is right in outline; however Columbus's 'Italian miles' reading of Alfraganus is the usual account, so this is fine. The real slip is the claimed 'true gap roughly 19,000 km' alongside the Americas 'about 4,500 km out'; the Americas are much closer than 4,500 km at the Caribbean (~6,000-7,000 km from the Canaries to the Bahamas), so the figure is loose.

errors.claim: Step 9: Columbus used 'the shortest estimate of a degree of longitude' and Step 5 gives 3,700 km to Japan while Step 9 gives 2,400 nm (~4,450 km)
errors.fix: The two figures for Columbus's estimated distance are inconsistent; the commonly cited value is about 2,400 nautical miles (~4,400 km) to Japan from the Canaries.

errors.claim: Step 8: 'Castile was shut out of that Atlantic-African road by the Portuguese monopoly' and the Mamluk-Venetian chain 'was the only other way'
errors.fix: Overstated: Castile was restricted by the 1479 Treaty of Alcáçovas, but the Mamluk-Venetian route was not the only alternative to the Cape, and the framing glosses over the Portuguese-Castilian treaty basis.

grade.best: It corrects the premise at once and shows that the real dispute was Columbus's small Earth versus his critics' correct larger one, with Irving, Draper and White tracing how the myth was made.
grade.worst: Tighten the numbers: the answer gives inconsistent estimates of Columbus's distance to Japan (3,700 km versus 2,400 nm) and loosely states the Americas' distance, and the economic steps stray from the question.

errors.claim: Stalin stayed with Alexei Troyanovsky near Schönbrunn; also lodged at 'Schönbrunnerstraße-area' and 'Stumpergasse' addresses; Hitler and Stalin lived about 6 km apart
errors.fix: Stalin stayed with Troyanovsky at Schönbrunner Schlossstrasse; the Stumpergasse address is unrelated and the answer's lodging claims are inconsistent and shaky.

errors.claim: Trotsky edited the Pravda he published for Russian workers; spent much of 1912-13 as a Balkan war correspondent so may not have been home
errors.fix: Trotsky's Vienna Pravda (1908-12) was a separate paper from the Bolshevik Pravda; he was in the Balkans for Kievskaya Mysl 1912-13, a defensible point, but the editing claim is vague.

errors.claim: Hitler lived at the Männerheim on Meldemannstraße from February 1910 to May 1913 and was in Vienna in January and February 1913 as 'aged 23' and also '24-year-old'
errors.fix: Hitler turned 24 in April 1913; he was 23 in winter. The answer is internally inconsistent on his age.

grade.best: It separates overlap in time and city from an actual meeting, flags the Café Central and Schönbrunn encounter stories as legend, and names the unknowns.
grade.worst: It is padded with tangential steps on demography, the Ringstrasse and Habsburg politics, and it hedges on Trotsky's 1907-1914 Vienna residence and Tito's presence instead of stating them cleanly.
